title: Wuppertal’s trains have hung beneath a rail above a river since 1901

cover.alt: Seen from below, a long dark steel track bends away over a river, carried on slanting green steel legs, with a small red train hanging from it in the distance.

body: The **Wuppertal Schwebebahn** in western Germany opened on 1 March 1901 and is the oldest electric elevated railway with hanging cars in the world. Instead of sitting on rails, each car hangs from motor-driven wheels that roll along a **single rail** fixed underneath a steel frame, so the whole line stands in the air on 486 pillars and bridge sections. For about 10 km of its 13.3 km route it runs over the River Wupper, roughly 12 m above the water, and the rest hangs about 8 m over a road.

slides.alt: Looking up from the riverbank under a long steel track on slanting green legs, a red train appears round a bend, glides overhead hanging from the track, and heads on towards a station beside a large stone building, with people walking below.
slides.caption: A Schwebebahn (hanging railway) train swings in above the River Wupper, passes overhead hanging from its rail and heads on into Wuppertal Hauptbahnhof station.

slides.heading: What the 13.3 km line hangs over
slides.note: About 12 m above the river and about 8 m above the road; 20 stations in all

slides.question: Roughly how many passengers a year did the Schwebebahn carry, according to its 2008 annual report?
slides.explanation: About 25 million a year, or some 82,000 a day. A whole trip end to end takes about 30 minutes, at up to 60 km/h.

slides.question: Where do the hanging trains get their electricity?
options: A live rail below the running rail
slides.explanation: Their wheels are driven by electric motors running on 600 or 750 volts DC, fed from a live rail just below the rail the wheels roll on.
